quartiers:Port Héraclea.name: Port Héraclea
quartiers:Port Héraclea.teaser: Eleven hundred masts in a bay the Romans already used, and the morning catch sold on the quay
quartiers:Port Héraclea.story: The bay faces south, screened from the Mistral by the Maures, and ships have sheltered here since antiquity. Scholars generally identify it with Heraclea Caccabaria, a stop named in the Roman Antonine Itinerary. Nothing ancient stands above the water: what has lasted is the shelter. Today it is Port Héraclea, about 1,100 berths for boats of 7 to 24 metres in a basin 2.5 metres deep, run since July 2018 by a public company, the SPL Port Héraclea, formed when the private and public harbours merged. Mid-morning the fishermen tie up at Quai Marc Pajot; their stand has its own table card.
quartiers:Port Héraclea.why: Come at ten for the boats and the quay, then come back at dusk when the masts tick in the breeze and the bars open.

quartiers:Pardigon.name: Pardigon
quartiers:Pardigon.teaser: Meadow, reeds and two Roman wine estates behind the beach: the one stretch of this bay nobody may build on
quartiers:Pardigon.story: Where Cavalaire's sand runs out to the east, the houses stop and a green bowl of old fields and wet meadow opens up under the Maures, crossed by the Carrade stream. After years of court fights the Conseil d'État declared it a 'site remarquable du littoral' (unbuildable), and in January 2011 the Conservatoire du littoral made it inalienable. Excavations in the 1980s found two Roman villas, one on each side of the Carrade and one in each commune. The La Croix-Valmer one, Pardigon II, covers about 3,500 square metres and is described as one of the largest maritime villas on the coast of Roman Gaul, built around AD 20-40.
quartiers:Pardigon.why: Walk from the beach into the meadow in the early morning, when herons work the reeds and nothing behind you is concrete.

quartiers:The young town.name: The young town
quartiers:The young town.teaser: A chapel of 1910 and a commune of 1929: Cavalaire is younger than many of its visitors' grandparents
quartiers:The young town.story: Cavalaire looks like an old fishing village and is nothing of the kind. Until 1929 it was a hamlet of Gassin, the hill village above; that year it became a commune of its own and took the name Cavalaire-sur-Mer. Its parish church tells the same story in stone. Saint-Laurent on Avenue Pierre Rameil began in 1910 as a modest chapel that answered to Gassin, was enlarged in 1932 and only became a parish in 1960. Tourism did the rest: the town was classified a beach resort in 1956 and a Station de Tourisme in 2013.

quartiers:La Croix-Valmer and Gigaro.name: La Croix-Valmer and Gigaro
quartiers:La Croix-Valmer and Gigaro.teaser: A village named after an emperor's vision, its vines running down to the beach where the wild coast begins
quartiers:La Croix-Valmer and Gigaro.story: La Croix-Valmer takes its name from a legend: in 312, on his way to fight Maxentius, the emperor Constantine is said to have seen a cross in the sky here with the words 'In hoc signo vinces'. A stone cross raised on 16 April 1893 marks the supposed spot; several other places claim the same vision. The village was La Croix de Cavalaire and La Croix des Mimosas before it settled on La Croix-Valmer in 1934. It sits on a hill above its vineyards. Below, Gigaro beach ends at the start of the coast path to the capes, and the Plage du Débarquement continues Cavalaire's sand to the west.
quartiers:La Croix-Valmer and Gigaro.why: Go down to Gigaro in late afternoon: the eastern corner of the beach is where the protected coast begins.

quartiers:Le Rayol-Canadel.name: Le Rayol-Canadel
quartiers:Le Rayol-Canadel.teaser: A 1925 resort where the Maures drop straight into the sea, with a flowered stairway down to the beach
quartiers:Le Rayol-Canadel.story: West of Cavalaire the Corniche des Maures climbs, and the forest comes right down to the water. Around 1925 a property company laid out Le Rayol-Canadel as a seaside resort on these slopes, and its signature piece is still in use: a long flowered stairway from the road to the Rayol beach, its low walls built of Maures schist and set with terracotta vases, topped by the round concrete pergola of the Pateck on stone columns. The architect is not known; stairway and pergola have been listed historic monuments since December 1989. The Canadel beach lies just east, and above the village the Col du Canadel opens onto the ridge.

curiosities:The hill fort over the bay.name: The hill fort on Montjean
curiosities:The hill fort over the bay.teaser: Two thousand five hundred years before the marina, a Ligurian people watched the bay from a dry-stone fort
curiosities:The hill fort over the bay.story: Long before Greek or Roman ships put in, the people of the Maures built a dry-stone fortress on the Montjean ridge above Cavalaire. The heritage register describes it as a Ligurian oppidum occupied from the 6th to the 4th century BC. It was excavated between 1963 and 1979 and entered on the supplementary list of historic monuments in 1996. Then villas went up on the summit and destroyed part of it: only a narrow strip of ground is left intact. Finds from the dig are shown at the town's archaeology room. Walk up anyway for the view: the whole bay and the Gulf of Saint-Tropez.
curiosities:The hill fort over the bay.why: Climb it on a clear winter morning: the people who built it chose the spot for the same view of the bay you get.
facts: About a 45-minute walk from the Col du Canadel; free and open all year, per the tourist office (Oct 2026)

curiosities:The train that made the town.name: The train that made the town
curiosities:The train that made the town.teaser: A coastal railway built the resort, ran for sixty years and left behind a station you can walk into
curiosities:The train that made the town.story: Cavalaire owes its first villas and bathers to a narrow coastal railway. The Chemins de Fer du Sud de la France won the contract for a line from Saint-Raphaël to Hyères and Toulon, began work in 1882, and Cavalaire's station dates from 1890. The Second World War brought sabotage and bombing, the car took the rest of the traffic, and in 1949 the line was taken up and replaced by buses. Along the coast its route survives as roads and cycle tracks. Cavalaire's station still stands on Place de la Gare and is now the town's exhibition hall.
curiosities:The train that made the town.why: Next time you pass the bus station, look up: the town's first front door is still standing.

curiosities:The seafarers' chapel of 163.name: The lost seafarers' chapel
curiosities:The seafarers' chapel of 163.teaser: Cavalaire once had a sailors' chapel older than the town by three centuries; nothing of it stands
curiosities:The seafarers' chapel of 163.story: The town's own history tells of a seafarers' chapel, Notre-Dame de l'Annonciade, built in 1639 when Cavalaire was a handful of fishermen and a landing place belonging to Gassin. It is said to have been shut in 1793, during the Revolution, and left to fall down, and its ruins to have been cleared away during the German occupation of the Second World War. That makes the young town's oldest building one that no longer exists. Do not confuse it with the Annonciade in Saint-Tropez, a different chapel that now holds the painters' museum (its own card, under Culture).
curiosities:The seafarers' chapel of 163.why: Ask at the médiathèque what the town knows of it: it is the oldest name in Cavalaire's history with nothing to show for it.

curiosities:A drowned fleet under the sw.name: The wreck of the Togo
curiosities:A drowned fleet under the sw.teaser: A 76-metre cargo cut in two by a German mine in 1918 lies on the sand of the bay, bow towards the beach
curiosities:A drowned fleet under the sw.story: The sheltered bay is one of this coast's serious wreck-diving grounds, with more than a dozen wrecks. The best known is the Togo, a 76-metre cargo ship launched in 1882 as the Ville de Valence and renamed in 1912 when the Genoese company Ilva bought her. On 12 May 1918 she hit a 150-kilo mine laid by the German submarine UC 35, broke in two and sank at once. She lay forgotten until 1977, when the biologist and diver Richard Calmes found her while laying buoys for a Club Nautique de Cavalaire regatta. She rests flat on a gently sloping sand bottom, west of the Pointe Dubreuil, bow pointing at Cavalaire beach, in red gorgonians.
curiosities:A drowned fleet under the sw.why: Even if you never dive, look out from Cavalaire beach: the Togo's bow points straight at you from the bottom of the bay.
facts: Only with a dive centre and at advanced level (French level 3 or equivalent): 45 to 61 metres, several dives to see it all; the town publishes a diving brochure

curiosities:The tuna traps of the gulf.name: The tuna traps of the gulf
curiosities:The tuna traps of the gulf.teaser: Brigitte Bardot's house is named after a fishing net: the madrague, a maze that caught the bluefin
curiosities:The tuna traps of the gulf.story: For centuries the Provençal coast caught bluefin tuna in the madrague, a fixed labyrinth of nets set from spring across the fish's path, chamber after chamber, until the last one, where the fishermen hauled them out. The method goes back a very long way around the Mediterranean, and it peaked here from the 17th century before fading through the 19th. Old fishing leases place four madragues around the Gulf of Saint-Tropez: Cap de la Moutte, Pampelonne, Les Canebiers and La Nartelle. None is set today. The word stayed behind in place names, most famously La Madrague, Bardot's house on the Canebiers bay.
curiosities:The tuna traps of the gulf.why: On the Canebiers path, read the name La Madrague as a fishing word first, a film star's address second.
facts: Walk the coast path at Les Canebiers, past the cove of La Madrague, on the Saint-Tropez side of the peninsula

curiosities:The pointu.name: The pointu
curiosities:The pointu.teaser: Pointed at both ends and painted bright: the small wooden boat of the Provençal fishermen
curiosities:The pointu.story: The pointu is the small fishing boat of this coast: wooden, decked, four to nine metres long, pointed at both ends so it rides a following sea and lands easily on a beach. Most now carry a motor where the lateen sail used to be. Along the Marseille shore the same family of boat is called a barquette, and a Marseille specialist says the word 'pointu' belongs to the Var and further east; the barquette has a more curved bow and stern. Boatyards in Marseille still teach the old way of building them, and about a hundred barquettes still sail there in the traditional manner.
curiosities:The pointu.why: Ask a fisherman on the quay whether his boat is a pointu or a barquette, and listen to the answer.
facts: Look for them in the small-boat moorings of the ports on this coast, from Cavalaire to Saint-Tropez

culture:Domaine du Rayol.name: Domaine du Rayol
culture:Domaine du Rayol.teaser: Chile, California, the Cape and Australia planted on one Var hillside running down to the sea
culture:Domaine du Rayol.story: In the years after 1908 the businessman Alfred Courmes bought wild maquis above the Baie du Figuier and had the architect Guillaume Tronchet build villas, a classical pergola (1910) and the Hôtel de la Mer. The aircraft builder Henry Potez took it over in 1940. By the 1980s it faced a 284-flat development; residents formed Les Amis du Rayol-Canadel in 1980 and the Conservatoire du littoral bought the 20-hectare estate in 1989. The gardener Gilles Clément then planted about 7 hectares with the floras of the world's dry-summer climates, so a Cape protea grows near a Californian ceanothus and a Chilean puya on the same slope.

culture:Musée de l'Annonciade.teaser: A former chapel on the Saint-Tropez harbour, hung with Signac, Matisse and Bonnard before the yachts came
culture:Musée de l'Annonciade.story: Saint-Tropez drew painters before it drew yachts. Paul Signac sailed in on his own boat in 1892, stayed, and pulled his friends south: Henri-Edmond Cross, Matisse, Bonnard, Marquet. The museum, founded in 1922 and housed in a former chapel by the port, holds the work that came out of those years, Pointillist dots, Nabi interiors and Fauve colour, much of it painted within sight of the building. It is a small museum and easy to see in an hour, and the paintings of the old harbour make a good pair with the real one outside the door.

culture:Alpha — the landing beach.name: Alpha, the landing beach
culture:Alpha — the landing beach.teaser: The other D-Day came ashore on this sand at 8am on 15 August 1944; today it is parasols and pédalos
culture:Alpha — the landing beach.story: On 15 August 1944 the bay was Alpha, the westernmost sector of Operation Dragoon, the Allied landing in Provence. At H-Hour, 8am, the US 3rd Infantry Division went in: its 7th Infantry Regiment on Alpha Red in the bay of Cavalaire, its 15th on Alpha Yellow near Pampelonne. Resistance was light and mines were the real danger. That assault shore is mostly the beach just east, in La Croix-Valmer, since renamed the Plage du Débarquement. The next evening, from about 7pm on 16 August, General de Lattre's French Army B began landing at Cavalaire, and on the 17th the 1st Free French Division regrouped at La Croix-Valmer.
culture:Alpha — the landing beach.why: Stand at the granite columns at the harbour entrance, then walk east along the sand to the Plage du Débarquement: one bay, two days.

provisioning:Château Minuty.teaser: The Gassin estate behind the gulf's best-known pale rosé, now part of Moët Hennessy
provisioning:Château Minuty.story: Château Minuty, at Gassin on the hill above the gulf, is another of the 1955 Crus Classés (see the Drink card). For decades it was the Matton family's house; in February 2023 Moët Hennessy, the wine and spirits arm of LVMH, took a majority stake, with Jean-Étienne and François Matton staying on to run it, Decanter reported. walks:Le Sentier des Trois Caps.name: Le Sentier des Trois Caps
walks:Le Sentier des Trois Caps.teaser: From Gigaro to Cap Taillat and back through the cork oaks: the longest wild shore left on the peninsula
walks:Le Sentier des Trois Caps.story: Start at the eastern end of Gigaro beach, where the sand gives way to rock and the yellow marks of the coastal path begin. The path is the old customs track, cut along the shore so that patrols could watch every cove, and it still goes where they went: up over Cap Lardier, down to the long Briande bay, on to the sand neck of Cap Taillat. From there the loop turns inland and climbs back through cork oak, pine and cistus. What the walk shows is a boundary: the villas stop where the Conservatoire du littoral's land begins, and from there to Taillat there is almost nothing built. The third cape, Camarat with its lighthouse, stays ahead of you on the Ramatuelle side.
walks:Le Sentier des Trois Caps.why: The only way to see this shore whole is on foot; leave the beach day for the coves you pass.

walks:Cap Lardier's crest.name: Cap Lardier's crest
walks:Cap Lardier's crest.teaser: Mid-walk, the cape's high point opens a half-circle of sea from Camarat's lighthouse to the Îles d'Hyères
walks:Cap Lardier's crest.story: Cap Lardier was classified as a protected site in 1966, and from 1978 the Conservatoire du littoral bought its pine massif, about 300 hectares, parcel by parcel. The result is the longest protected stretch of shore of the three capes, some 6 km, and from the crest you take it in at once: the Camarat lighthouse to the east, Cap Taillat's low headland below, the Îles du Levant and the other Îles d'Hyères offshore, and the whole bay of Cavalaire behind you. The Bastide Blanche and La Croix vines run almost to the cliff edge. There is no road to the point.
walks:Cap Lardier's crest.why: The one place on the walk where you see why the capes stayed empty: green on one side, built on every other.

walks:Sentier du Fenouillet.name: Sentier du Fenouillet
walks:Sentier du Fenouillet.teaser: Cavalaire's own headland walk: cork oak, strawberry trees and coves, from Bonporteau beach on foot
walks:Sentier du Fenouillet.story: The Fenouillet headland is the Domaine Foncin. In 1977 Mireille Foncin, daughter of the geographer Pierre Foncin, a founder of the Alliance Française, left the land to the Conservatoire du littoral, one of the first gifts it ever received, and that is why this piece of the Corniche des Maures has no villas. The path leaves Plage de Bonporteau, follows the cliffs towards Pointe du Dattier with views to the Îles d'Hyères and back to Cap Lardier, then returns through a shaded, damp valley. Come in autumn: the strawberry trees flower and fruit at the same time, and the maquis smells of honey.
walks:Sentier du Fenouillet.why: No car needed: the maquis of the Maures begins on the edge of town.

calas:Cap Taillat.name: Cap Taillat
calas:Cap Taillat.teaser: A rocky headland tied to the shore by a lane of sand, with a different bay breaking on each side
calas:Cap Taillat.story: Cap Taillat was once an island. The currents built a tombolo, a strip of fine sand no wider than a lane, that now ties it to the mainland, with the Baie de Briande on the La Croix-Valmer side and the Baie de Bonporteau (Ramatuelle's, not Cavalaire's) on the other. Wind from east or west moves the sand constantly and winter storms eat at it, so the dune is fenced with chestnut ganivelles. The Conservatoire du littoral owns some 142 hectares here. On 24 July 2017 a fire ran from Gigaro to L'Escalet and burned the cape to ash; after about 2,000 dead trees were felled the path reopened eight months later on a new line. The maquis came back fast; the umbrella pines will take decades.
calas:Cap Taillat.why: Stand on the sand neck and swim on whichever side the wind is not blowing.
facts: On foot only: the shortest walk in is from the Plage de l'Escalet car park, Ramatuelle; or the long coastal path from Gigaro; or by sea

calas:Plage de la Briande.name: Plage de la Briande
calas:Plage de la Briande.teaser: La Croix-Valmer's wildest beach: a long curve of sand with pines behind it and no road in
calas:Plage de la Briande.story: Briande is the last beach of La Croix-Valmer, a long curve of pale sand on the western flank of Cap Taillat, backed by thick maquis and umbrella pines with nothing built behind it. No road reaches it, so the only way in is the coastal path, about 45 minutes on foot from the southern car park at L'Escalet, and it lies inside the protected Lardier and Taillat corridor, which means it will never be built on or serviced. On a weekday out of August you can have a stretch of it to yourself. Naturists use the wild coves along the walk, but Briande is not an official naturist beach: read the signs.
calas:Plage de la Briande.why: The long walk in keeps the crowds down; that is the whole point of the place.

calas:The douaniers' coves.teaser: Three coves on the customs path from Gigaro: the tiny Douane, Jovat with its ruined cabin, and wild Brouis
calas:The douaniers' coves.story: Leave Gigaro by its quiet eastern corner and the coastal path begins to thread small coves most visitors never learn the names of. First the crique de la Douane, tiny and close to the start. Then Jovat, sandier, with the ruins of an old fishing cabin above the water. Then Brouis, the wildest, where you are more or less certain to be alone. All three sit on protected land and in a Natura 2000 zone, which is why they stay calm even in August while Gigaro fills. The path itself is the Trois Caps walk, under its own card.
calas:The douaniers' coves.why: Walk past the first cove; the farther you go, the emptier the sand.

calas:Bonporteau.name: Bonporteau
calas:Bonporteau.teaser: Cavalaire's wild cove, with a free buoyed snorkel trail laid over the seagrass just offshore
calas:Bonporteau.story: A steep footpath from the Avenue de Bonporteau drops through eucalyptus and palms to a cove of fine sand ringed with rock and tamarisk, with picnic tables in the pine shade. Just offshore, seven coloured buoys and underwater panels mark a snorkel trail over the Posidonia meadows, the nursery of this coast, where saupes, bream and girelles drift and a young grouper sometimes hangs under a ledge. It lies in the marine area of the Port-Cros national park and is free to anyone who can swim with mask and fins. In summer a state-qualified guide leads it; the park's guided mornings have been on Tuesdays. The buoys are in from June to September, so in late October the trail is closed for the year.
calas:Bonporteau.why: A free underwater trail on the edge of town, unsupervised and quiet while the main beach fills.

calas:The Rayol coves.name: The Rayol coves
calas:The Rayol coves.teaser: White-sand coves under the Corniche des Maures, reached by paths steep enough to keep them wild
calas:The Rayol coves.story: West of Cavalaire the Massif des Maures drops almost straight into the sea, and the coast road strings small pine-backed beaches between the Rayol and Le Lavandou: Le Rayol, Le Canadel, Cavalière, Pramousquier. Between them hide smaller coves such as the Plage du Figuier, white sand and clear water over rock and seagrass, reached by steep and sometimes unmarked paths that locals call sportif. The slope is the protection. In autumn and winter you may find the sand lined with brown banks of dead Posidonia leaves; they are a sign of a healthy seabed, not a dirty beach, and they protect the sand from storms.
calas:The Rayol coves.why: Greener and far less built-up than the club beaches east of the peninsula, ten to twenty minutes by car.

calas:Le Sentier Marin du Rayol.name: Le Sentier Marin du Rayol
calas:Le Sentier Marin du Rayol.teaser: A guided snorkel over the seagrass of the Baie du Figuier, from the Domaine du Rayol's own beach
calas:Le Sentier Marin du Rayol.story: Below the Domaine du Rayol the bay of the Figuier is protected land and sea, and in summer the estate runs a guided snorkel over it in wetsuit, mask and fins. The guide takes small groups over Posidonia meadows, urchins and damselfish, and with luck an octopus. The one thing to carry home: Posidonia is not a seaweed but a flowering plant that grows under the sea, a great oxygen maker and the nursery for much of what you see. The 2026 season ran from 18 June to 13 September, so it reopens next June; the garden itself has its own card under Culture.
calas:Le Sentier Marin du Rayol.why: The easiest way to see the seabed of the Hyères islands without leaving the mainland.

avoid:Reading the winter seafront as emp.teaser: Shuttered terraces in winter do not mean there is nothing here: the town's larder keeps going
avoid:Reading the winter seafront as emp.story: From late October the beach restaurants and most summer terraces close, and by January the seafront looks shut and the port is quiet. The Wednesday market on Place Jean Moulin trades all year, the fishermen still sell on the quay on mornings when the boats have been out, the Domaine du Rayol garden stays open on winter hours, and in February the mimosa turns the corniche yellow.

craft:What is sold as Provençal craft.teaser: The soap stamped Marseille and the lavender sachet may have come from much further than the stall
craft:What is sold as Provençal craft.story: The seafront souvenir shops sell two things above all as Provence in a bag: soap stamped 'savon de Marseille' and lavender. Neither name guarantees where it came from. Savon de Marseille has no protected definition in law; the traditional recipe is about 72 percent vegetable oil with no animal fat, perfume or colouring, yet bars carrying the stamp are made in Asia, sometimes from tallow. Lavender is similar. Bulgaria, not France, is now the world's largest producer of lavender oil, and sachets and soaps sold on Provençal stalls may hold lavandin, the coarser hybrid, or synthetic scent.
craft:What is sold as Provençal craft.why: Read the back of the packet, not the front: ingredients and origin tell you what the stamp does not.
facts: Turn the soap over: look for vegetable oils only (olive first), no tallow ('sodium tallowate'), and a maker's town; on lavender look for 'lavande fine' or the AOP Huile essentielle de lavande de Haute-Provence

drink:Côtes de Provence rosé.name: Côtes de Provence rosé
drink:Côtes de Provence rosé.teaser: Pale by design and dry to the last drop: the bottle on nearly every table round the bay
drink:Côtes de Provence rosé.story: The paleness is a choice made in the cellar. Côtes de Provence rosé is pressed straight from the grape, or left on the skins for only a few hours, then fermented cold, so the juice takes the faintest onion-skin tint while the wine stays dry. It is the great appellation of the region, and rosé makes up close to nine bottles in ten of what it produces. Around the bay the vines grow within sight of the sea, and the better bottles finish with a salty edge. It does not keep: the newest vintage is the one to drink, cold, this year.
drink:Côtes de Provence rosé.why: Order the youngest vintage on the list and send back anything served warm.
facts: Pale pink; red currant, citrus peel, a dry, faintly saline finish

drink:Cru Classé rosé.name: Cru Classé rosé
drink:Cru Classé rosé.teaser: Provence ranked its own estates in 1955; eighteen still print 'Cru Classé', two of them close by
drink:Cru Classé rosé.story: In 1955 a ministerial decree classified a set of Côtes de Provence estates as crus classés, decades before the appellation itself existed. Of that list, eighteen still use the words on their labels, and two are within half an hour of Cavalaire: Domaine de la Croix above La Croix-Valmer and Château Minuty at Gassin. The rank was given on reputation and standing at the time, not after a blind tasting, and it has never been revised. A Cru Classé rosé usually has more grip and density than the house pink, and costs more.
drink:Cru Classé rosé.why: Taste one Cru Classé next to a plain Côtes de Provence from the same village and judge the gap yourself.
facts: Pale, but fuller and firmer than the house pink; more length

drink:Tibouren.name: Tibouren
drink:Tibouren.teaser: The peninsula's own grape gives a rosé that smells of hot pine and salt, not boiled sweets
drink:Tibouren.story: Tibouren is the old grape of this stretch of coast, long planted around Saint-Tropez and now rare elsewhere. It makes a savoury rosé with a faint orange cast, smelling of garrigue herbs rather than strawberries. The place to taste it is the sandy strip between Cap Lardier and Cap Taillat, where Bastide Blanche's vines run almost to the cliff path and the wind off the sea scours them. Bastide Blanche shares its owners with Domaine de la Croix, so treat the two as one house, not rivals. Both it and La Tourraque, inside the three-capes site at Ramatuelle, are certified organic.
drink:Tibouren.why: Drink a Tibouren rosé beside a supermarket Provence and you will taste what 'saline' means.
facts: Pale with an orange tint; garrigue, dried herbs, pine resin, a salty finish

drink:Rolle, the white.name: Rolle, the white
drink:Rolle, the white.teaser: Vermentino under its Provençal name: citrus pith and sea spray, and rarely sold outside the region
drink:Rolle, the white.story: Rolle is what Provence calls Vermentino, the grape that also makes the whites of Corsica and Liguria. Near this coast it gives a white with the bitterness of citrus pith and a mineral, sea-spray finish, and it is the wine for the morning catch from the fishermen's quay, grilled or raw. Provence makes far less white than rosé, and most of it is drunk here, so a good bottle of Rolle is easier to find on a village shelf than on a wine list abroad.
drink:Rolle, the white.why: Buy a bottle of local Rolle for the boat; you will struggle to find the same one at home.
facts: Pale gold; lemon pith, white flowers, a bitter-almond, salty finish

drink:The red for a cool evening.name: The red for a cool evening
drink:The red for a cool evening.teaser: Provence is not only pink: Mourvèdre and Syrah for the night the mistral turns the deck cold
drink:The red for a cool evening.story: Most visitors leave Provence without opening a red, and miss the wine for an October night. Mourvèdre and Syrah on the warmer soils give a dark red that smells of herbs, black olive and leather, built for lamb, daube or a grilled steak after the wind has cleared the sky. The one fix most people need is the temperature: serve it lightly cool, around 15°C, not at the heat of a summer cabin, which makes these reds taste of alcohol.
drink:The red for a cool evening.why: Put the bottle in the fridge for twenty minutes before dinner.
facts: Deep red; black fruit, garrigue herbs, black olive, leather

drink:Pastis.name: Pastis
drink:Pastis.teaser: One measure, five of cold water, and the glass turns cloudy: the coast's apéritif, distilled in the hills
drink:Pastis.story: The ritual does not change: a measure of pastis, about five of cold water poured over it, then ice, and the clear spirit turns milky yellow, the 'louche'. It is drunk in the shade before lunch or at six in the evening. Most bars pour Ricard or Pastis 51, both from Marseille. Henri Bardouin is the one to ask for: Distilleries et Domaines de Provence blend it from more than 65 plants and spices, where the big brands lean on anise and liquorice. It is made inland at Forcalquier, in Haute-Provence. The coast owns the ritual; the hills make the bottle.
drink:Pastis.why: Ask for a Bardouin and add the water yourself from the carafe, ice last.
facts: Amber turning cloudy with water; star anise, liquorice, fennel and herbs
Pastis; Bardouin lists its herbs on the back

bars:Bar 1904, La Messardière.story: La Messardière is a turreted château in its own park on the hill above Saint-Tropez, given as a wedding present by the cognac merchant Gabriel Dupuy d'Angeac to his daughter Louise. bars:La Rhumerie.story: After dark Cavalaire's energy gathers in the gap between the moored boats and the Nouveau Port quay, and La Rhumerie is where it ends up. It is the nearest thing the town has to a club, and it is honestly a bar. Its real advantage is the calendar: it trades from February to November, so it is still open while most of the seafront has shut. For an actual nightclub you have to go to Saint-Tropez.

listening:No hi-fi bar on this bay.story: We looked for a listening bar between Le Lavandou and Saint-Tropez, the kind of room with a serious sound system, a wall of records and a bartender who keeps quiet while the side plays. What this bay has instead is music in the open air: municipal concerts on the Cavalaire seafront and the port in summer, theatre and classical nights on the hills of Ramatuelle, chamber music in a Saint-Tropez estate garden. listening:Jazz à Ramatuelle.name: Jazz à Ramatuelle
listening:Jazz à Ramatuelle.teaser: Forty years of late-June jazz under the cicadas, and no edition in 2026
listening:Jazz à Ramatuelle.story: The festival began in the mid-1980s with a local postman, Denis Antoine, a jazz obsessive who talked the saxophonist Guy Lafitte into bringing real players to his village. For four decades it filled Ramatuelle's open-air Théâtre de Verdure in late June: stone tiers, pines behind the stage, cicadas still going when the first set starts. The last edition we can document ran 24 to 28 June 2025. The organisers then announced there would be no festival in 2026, and Ramatuelle's own summer programme said the same. Nothing has been announced for 2027 yet. Treat it as a hope, not a plan.
listening:Jazz à Ramatuelle.why: If it comes back, it is the gulf's most unpretentious jazz week; watch jazzaramatuelle.com before booking a June trip around it.

listening:Festival de Ramatuelle.name: Festival de Ramatuelle
listening:Festival de Ramatuelle.teaser: Twelve August nights of French stage stars in a hill village's open-air theatre, one show a night
listening:Festival de Ramatuelle.story: In 1985 the actor Jean-Claude Brialy and Jacqueline Franjou started a summer festival in Ramatuelle in tribute to Gérard Philipe, the actor whose name the open-air theatre now carries. Forty-one summers on, the formula has hardly moved: one show a night at half past nine, the audience on tiers under the pines, comedy, plays and song by names French audiences know. The actor Michel Boujenah is artistic director. The 2026 edition opened with a classical prelude from 29 July, including Beethoven's Ninth, and then ran its twelve main evenings from 1 to 12 August, with Manu Payet on the first night and Jeanne Cherhal on 8 August.
listening:Festival de Ramatuelle.why: Book a single night in early June and go up early: dinner in the village first, then the walk to the theatre at dusk.

listening:Les Nuits du Château de la Mou.name: Les Nuits de la Moutte
listening:Les Nuits du Château de la Mou.teaser: Chamber music and cello in the grounds of a statesman's estate at Saint-Tropez, early August
listening:Les Nuits du Château de la Mou.story: The Château de la Moutte sits in its own pines and palms on the eastern edge of Saint-Tropez, the estate of Émile Ollivier, Napoleon III's last head of government. For eleven nights each August its private grounds open for music: classical, baroque, jazz and world, under trees rather than a roof. In 2026, its 51st year, the cellist Gautier Capuçon took over as artistic director and played the opening night himself on 1 August, with the pianist Jérôme Ducros; the festival ran to 11 August. In 2024 Capuçon had already carried his cello down to the sand for an evening called 'Un violoncelle sur le sable'.
listening:Les Nuits du Château de la Mou.why: The smallest, best-mannered audience of the gulf's summer, and the one night out that ends with the sea in earshot.

around:Gassin.name: Gassin
around:Gassin.teaser: A village built 200 metres up to watch for raiders, now the best free balcony over the gulf
around:Gassin.story: Gassin's founders put it on a steep knoll some 200 metres above the sea for one reason: to see sails coming before they landed. The height now serves the view. From the Place deï Barri, the old rampart terrace shaded by centuries-old hackberry trees, you turn slowly from the Bay of Saint-Tropez to the dark Maures ridge and out to the Îles d'Or. Then find the Androuno, a lane so tight that two people cannot pass: about 29 centimetres at its narrowest, the village says, and billed as one of the narrowest streets anywhere. Rue Rompe Cul, the steepest lane, earns its blunt name.
around:Gassin.why: Arrive an hour before sunset, when the day visitors have left and the terrace restaurants switch on their lamps.

around:Ramatuelle.name: Ramatuelle
around:Ramatuelle.teaser: Stone lanes wound in rings round a hilltop, vines down to Pampelonne, and Gérard Philipe in the cemetery
around:Ramatuelle.story: Ramatuelle is built in circles. The houses of the old village curl round the hilltop in tight rings, their back walls once doubling as the rampart, so the lanes run in arcs through vaulted passages and you keep coming back to where you started. Below, the slopes are vines, Côtes de Provence rosé country running down towards the long Pampelonne beach. The actor Gérard Philipe, who had a house here, was buried in the village cemetery in 1959, and the open-air theatre that carries his name hosts the summer festivals. In late October the lanes are quiet, the harvest is in and the shutters of the summer boutiques are down.
around:Ramatuelle.why: Come off season for the village itself: walk the rings slowly and let the lanes empty out around you.

around:Bormes-les-Mimosas.name: Bormes-les-Mimosas
around:Bormes-les-Mimosas.teaser: A stepped old town that turns yellow in February, voted France's favourite village in 2026
around:Bormes-les-Mimosas.story: Bormes climbs its hill above Le Lavandou in stairways and covered passages, and nearly every step has a pot, a vine or a palm on it: the village lives off a sheltered microclimate that lets plants from half the world grow in its lanes. Its name came from the mimosa that blazes yellow from January to March, and every mid-February since 1920 the Corso Fleuri parades mimosa-covered floats and throws the flowers into the crowd; the 83rd ran on 15 February 2026. The village joined Les Plus Beaux Villages de France on 21 September 2024, and in July 2026 the France 3 viewers' vote made it Village préféré des Français.
around:Bormes-les-Mimosas.why: Late January to February, for the mimosa; any other month, climb to the top of the old town for the view over Le Lavandou's bay.

around:Collobrières and La Verne.name: Collobrières and La Verne
around:Collobrières and La Verne.teaser: The Maures' chestnut village in its October fortnight, and a silent charterhouse in the cork oaks
around:Collobrières and La Verne.story: The road climbs into the Massif des Maures, cork oak and chestnut, until it drops into Collobrières, the chestnut village, where marrons glacés and chestnut cream are the local trade, and October brings its chestnut Sundays (the calendar has them). Further into the forest stands the Chartreuse de la Verne, a Carthusian monastery founded in 1170, its doorways cut from the Maures' green serpentine stone. Since 1983 a community of nuns of the Bethlehem family has lived there; visitors share only the church with them, in silence.
around:Collobrières and La Verne.why: Come in October for the chestnuts, and give the afternoon to La Verne while it keeps its autumn hours.

around:Porquerolles and Port-Cros.name: Porquerolles and Port-Cros
around:Porquerolles and Port-Cros.teaser: Two car-free islands on the horizon: one of beaches, vines and art, one of forest and the first marine park
around:Porquerolles and Port-Cros.story: From the Cavalaire seafront the Îles d'Hyères sit on the skyline, and on a calm day you can be on one by mid-morning. Porquerolles is the flat, generous one: white-sand beaches on the north shore, vineyards, bicycles, and the Fondation Carmignac's art villa among the pines. Port-Cros is the steep, wooded one, without cars or bikes, ringed by water clear enough to read the bottom. It became a national park on 14 December 1963, a gift of its last private owners, the Henry family, to the State, and the park calls itself the pioneer of Europe's marine parks. Walk ten minutes from either quay and the crowd thins out.
around:Porquerolles and Port-Cros.why: Take the first boat, walk away from the harbour at once, and swim where the path ends.
facts: From Cavalaire's port the Vedettes Îles d'Or boats ran roughly May to late August in 2026, and from La Croix-Valmer to late September: over for this year.
